clinicalPearls: Most severe congenital demyelinating neuropathy, presenting at or shortly after birth with profound hypotonia and weakness (the floppy infant)
Results from a failure of Schwann cells to form myelin, associated with variants in EGR2, MPZ, PMP22 and related myelin genes
Neonates often have respiratory and feeding difficulties, areflexia and distal contractures (arthrogryposis) reflecting antenatal immobility
Nerve conduction studies show extremely slow, often barely detectable motor conduction velocities because myelin is essentially absent
Nerve biopsy reveals a striking lack of myelin with thin or absent sheaths and basal lamina onion bulbs, distinguishing hypomyelination from later demyelination
It represents the most severe end of the CMT1/Dejerine-Sottas spectrum and can be difficult to separate clinically from severe Dejerine-Sottas disease
Diagnosis combines the neonatal presentation, profoundly slow electrophysiology, biopsy findings and genetic confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy arises when variants in genes controlling myelin formation, notably the transcription factor EGR2 and the structural proteins encoded by MPZ and PMP22, prevent Schwann cells from myelinating peripheral axons during development. Unlike the demyelinating CMTs, in which myelin forms and is then lost, here myelin is never properly established, so nerves remain largely amyelinated with basal lamina onion bulbs. The near-complete absence of myelin abolishes efficient saltatory conduction, producing the extremely slow or unobtainable conduction velocities and the severe, early neuromuscular dysfunction. Antenatal weakness can lead to joint contractures.
additionalDifferentials: Spinal muscular atrophy presenting as a floppy infant
Congenital myopathies and congenital myasthenic syndromes
Metabolic and mitochondrial disorders causing neonatal hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies showing profoundly slow or absent responses
Sural nerve biopsy demonstrating amyelination and basal lamina onion bulbs
Sequencing of EGR2, MPZ, PMP22 and a broad neuropathy panel
Respiratory and swallowing assessment in the neonate
Genetic testing for spinal muscular atrophy and other floppy-infant causes
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure requiring urgent support
Severe feeding and swallowing difficulty with aspiration risk
Rapidly progressive weakness in the neonatal period
Multiple joint contractures indicating significant antenatal involvement
reference.prognosis: Generally poor, with severe disability and, in the most affected infants, early respiratory compromise; outcome depends on the specific variant, and some children survive with major motor impairment.
pitfalls: Confusing hypomyelination (myelin never formed) with acquired or later-onset demyelination
Attributing neonatal hypotonia to a central cause without electrophysiology
Overlooking respiratory involvement, which drives early prognosis
Failing to distinguish it from spinal muscular atrophy and other floppy-infant syndromes
references: GeneReviews: EGR2- and Myelin-Gene-Related Congenital Hypomyelinating Neuropathy
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive, centred on early respiratory support with non-invasive or invasive ventilation for neonatal respiratory failure
Secure nutrition with nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding to overcome bulbar weakness and feeding difficulty
Physiotherapy, orthoses and serial casting or corrective surgery to manage arthrogrypotic contractures and preserve range of movement
Occupational therapy with adaptive seating and powered mobility aids for profound weakness
Ongoing surveillance for respiratory insufficiency, scoliosis and progressive orthopaedic deformity
Coordinated multidisciplinary neuromuscular team including neurology, respiratory, orthopaedics and rehabilitation
Genetic counselling with family and carrier testing given autosomal EGR2, MPZ and PMP22 inheritance, offering prenatal testing
Advance care planning with palliative input for the most severely affected infants
